title: Rising Action (22-40 mins):
use_cases: Use when developing the second act of a horror screenplay or novel
Configure when balancing quiet suspenseful moments with sudden bursts of terror
Implement when transitioning from an initial investigation to high-stakes survival
Use when planning character disappearances or deaths to increase urgency
Configure when establishing a significant narrative pivot or genre shift at the midpoint
content:
Shit just got real and the danger escalates — the protagonist(s) begin(s) investigating the entity or situation, leading to more terrifying encounters or discoveries. Characters may die or disappear here. The horror slowly reveals itself but remains partially hidden.

Tension-building scenes — alternate between quiet, suspenseful moments and bursts of terror (jump scares, eerie imagery). Build the protagonists’ sense of isolation, fear, and desperation.

Example: In “The Texas Chain Saw Massacre” (1974), Pam waits outside while Kirk goes into a house to try to buy some petrol for their van. Unbeknownst to Pam, Leatherface murders Kirk inside the house. When Pam goes inside, looking for Kirk, she stumbles across a room full of human and animal bones. Her fear and desperation grow, before she too is caught by Leatherface.

A major event or revelation changes the story’s direction as the protagonist faces a key challenge or learns crucial information, increasing the stakes.

Example: At the midpoint of “From Dusk Till Dawn” (1996), the main characters discover that the bar in which they’ve arranged a rendezvous is actually a hotbed of thirsty bloodsuckers. Now their main goal shifts from freedom to survival, and the film itself changes from violent crime thriller to full-on vampire gorefest.
